title: Mr. Toad
paragraphs: It was a bright morning in early summer. The river was back inside its usual banks and flowing at its usual pace, and a hot sun seemed to be tugging everything green and bushy and spiky up out of the ground toward it, as if on strings. Mole and Water Rat had been up since dawn, busy with all the jobs that come with boats and the start of the boating season: painting and varnishing, mending paddles, fixing cushions, searching for lost boat-hooks, and so on. They were finishing breakfast in their little parlor and eagerly talking over their plans for the day when a heavy knock came at the door.
“Bother!” said Rat, with egg all over him. “See who it is, Mole, there’s a good fellow, since you’ve finished eating.”
Mole went to answer the knock, and Rat heard him cry out in surprise. Then Mole threw the parlor door wide open and announced, with great importance, “Mr. Badger!”

This was truly remarkable, that Badger should pay a formal visit to them, or to anybody. If you wanted him badly, you generally had to catch him as he slipped quietly along a hedgerow in the early morning or the late evening, or else track him down at his own house in the middle of the Wood, which was a serious undertaking.
Badger tramped heavily into the room and stood looking at the two animals with a very grave expression. Rat let his egg-spoon drop onto the tablecloth and sat there with his mouth hanging open.
“The hour has come!” Badger said at last, with great solemnity.
“What hour?” asked Rat uneasily, glancing at the clock on the mantelpiece.

“You ought rather to ask _whose_ hour,” answered Badger. “Why, Toad’s hour! The hour of Toad! I said I would take him in hand as soon as winter was well over, and I am going to take him in hand today!”
“Toad’s hour, of course!” cried Mole with delight. “Hooray! It’s all coming back to me! _We’ll_ teach him how to be a sensible Toad!”

“This very morning,” Badger went on, settling into an armchair, “as I heard last night from a reliable source, another new and exceptionally powerful motor-car will arrive at Toad Hall, to be kept if he likes it or sent back if he doesn’t. At this very moment, perhaps, Toad is busy dressing himself in those uniquely hideous clothes he is so fond of, which turn him from a (fairly) good-looking Toad into a Thing that sends any decent-minded animal who meets it into a violent fit. We must get moving before it is too late. You two will come with me to Toad Hall at once, and the rescue will be carried out.”
“Right you are!” cried Rat, jumping up. “We’ll rescue the poor unhappy creature! We’ll convert him! By the time we’re through with him, he’ll be the most converted Toad there ever was!”

They set off up the road on their mission of mercy, with Badger in the lead. Animals who go about in company walk in a proper, sensible way, in single file, rather than sprawling across the whole road and being no use or help to each other if sudden trouble or danger comes.

They reached the carriage-drive of Toad Hall and found, just as Badger had expected, a shiny new motor-car of enormous size, painted bright red (Toad’s favorite color), standing in front of the house. As they came near the door, it was thrown open, and Mr. Toad, dressed in goggles, cap, leggings and an enormous overcoat, came swaggering down the steps, pulling on his long leather gloves.
“Well, hello! Come on, you fellows!” he called out merrily as soon as he spotted them. “You’ve arrived just in time to join me for a jolly—to go for a jolly—for a—er—jolly——”
His hearty voice faltered and died away as he saw the stern, unyielding looks on the faces of his silent friends, and his invitation was left unfinished.

Badger marched up the steps. “Take him indoors,” he told his companions sternly. Then, while Toad was shoved through the doorway, kicking and protesting, Badger turned to face the _chauffeur_ who had been left in charge of the brand-new motor-car.

“I’m afraid we won’t need you today,” he said. “Mr. Toad has changed his mind. He won’t be needing the car. Please understand that this is final. There’s no need for you to wait.” Then he followed the others inside and shut the door.
“Now then!” he said to Toad, when the four of them were standing together in the Hall. “First of all, take off those ridiculous things!”
“Shan’t!” answered Toad, with great spirit. “What is the meaning of this disgraceful outrage? I demand an explanation at once.”
“Take them off him, then, you two,” Badger ordered curtly.

They had to lay Toad out flat on the floor, kicking and shouting all sorts of names at them, before they could get properly to work. Then Rat sat on him, and Mole pulled his motoring clothes off him piece by piece, and they stood him up on his own two legs again. A good deal of his bluster seemed to have drained away along with his fine outfit. Now that he was just Toad, and no longer the Terror of the Highway, he giggled weakly and looked pleadingly from one to the other, as though he understood the situation perfectly.
“You knew it was bound to come to this sooner or later, Toad,” Badger explained severely.

Every warning we’ve given you, you’ve brushed aside. You’ve gone right on throwing away the money your father left you, and with your wild driving, your wrecks, and your arguments with the police, you’re dragging the good name of us animals through the mud around here. Being independent is fine, but we animals don’t stand by while a friend makes a fool of himself past a certain limit, and you’ve hit that limit. Now, in plenty of ways you’re a decent fellow, and I’d rather not be too hard on you. So I’ll try one last time to knock some sense into you. You’re coming with me to the smoking room, where you’re going to hear a few truths about yourself, and then we’ll find out whether the Toad who walks out of there is the same Toad who walked in.”
He gripped Toad firmly by the arm, marched him into the smoking-room, and pulled the door shut behind the two of them.
“_That’s_ no use!” said Rat scornfully. “_Talking_ to Toad will never cure him. He’ll _say_ anything.”

They settled into armchairs and waited patiently. Through the closed door they could just make out the long, steady drone of Badger’s voice, rising and falling in waves of speechmaking. After a while they noticed that the sermon was being interrupted every so often by long, drawn-out sobs, plainly coming from Toad’s chest. Toad was a soft-hearted, affectionate fellow, and very easily converted to any point of view—for the time being.

After about three-quarters of an hour the door opened, and Badger came back out, solemnly leading by the paw a very limp and dejected Toad. His skin hung loosely on him, his legs wobbled, and his cheeks were streaked with the tears that Badger’s moving speech had brought out so abundantly.

“Take a seat there, Toad,” said Badger in a kind voice, pointing at a chair. “My friends,” he continued, “it gives me great pleasure to announce that Toad has finally realized how wrong he has been. He feels genuine regret for the foolish way he used to behave, and he has agreed to swear off motor-cars altogether, once and for all. He has given me his solemn word on it.”
“That is very good news,” said Mole gravely.
“Very good news indeed,” remarked Rat doubtfully, “if only—_if_ only——”
As he said this, he was staring hard at Toad, and he couldn’t shake the idea that he could make out something like the faint glint of a twinkle in the animal’s eye, sad as it still was.

“There’s just one more thing to be done,” continued Badger, well pleased. “Toad, I want you to repeat solemnly, in front of your friends here, what you freely admitted to me in the smoking-room just now. First, you are sorry for what you’ve done, and you see how foolish it all was?”
A long, long silence followed. Toad glanced desperately in every direction while the other animals waited, grim and quiet. Finally he answered.
“No!” he answered, rather sulkily but firmly. “I am _not_ sorry. And it wasn’t madness in the least! It was absolutely glorious!”
“What?” cried Badger, thoroughly appalled. “You backsliding wretch, didn’t you just say, in there——”

“Oh yes, yes, in _there_,” Toad broke in, impatient. “In _there_ I’d have said anything. You’re so eloquent, dear Badger, so touching, so persuasive, and you argue every point so awfully well—in _there_ you can twist me around your finger, and you know you can. But since then I’ve been thinking it over, turning it all around in my head, and the truth is that I’m not one bit sorry or repentant, so there’s no earthly use pretending I am. Well, is there?”
“Then you won’t promise,” said Badger, “never to touch a motor-car again?”
“Certainly not!” Toad declared. “Quite the opposite! I give you my faithful promise that the moment I lay eyes on a motor-car, poop-poop! away I go in it!”
“Told you so, didn’t I?” Rat remarked to Mole.

“All right, then,” said Badger firmly, getting to his feet. “You refuse to be talked around, so we’ll see what force can accomplish. I was afraid it would come to this from the start. You’re always inviting the three of us to stay in this grand house of yours, Toad, and now we’re taking you up on it. We’ll leave once we’ve brought you around to a sensible way of thinking, and not one minute sooner. You two, march him upstairs and lock him in his bedroom while the rest of us work out a plan.”

“It’s for your own good, Toady, really it is,” said Rat kindly, while Toad kicked and struggled all the way up the stairs in the grip of his two loyal friends. “Just think of the fun we’ll have together, the way we used to, once you’re completely over this—this wretched fit of yours!”
“We’ll take great care of everything for you until you’re well, Toad,” said Mole, “and we’ll make sure your money isn’t wasted the way it has been.”
“No more unfortunate scrapes with the police, Toad,” said Rat, as they pushed him into his bedroom.
“And no more weeks in the hospital, Toad, being bossed around by lady nurses,” Mole added, turning the key in the lock.
They went back down the stairs, with Toad shouting abuse at them through the keyhole, and then the three friends met to discuss the situation.

“It’s going to be a tiresome business,” said Badger with a sigh. “I’ve never seen Toad so determined. However, we will see it through. He must never be left unguarded for a single moment. We shall have to take turns being with him, until the poison has worked its way out of his system.”

They arranged shifts accordingly. Each animal took a turn sleeping in Toad’s room at night, and they split the day up among them. At first Toad was certainly very trying for his careful guardians. When his violent fits came over him, he would line up bedroom chairs in a rough imitation of a motor-car and crouch on the front one, bent forward and staring fixedly ahead, making strange and ghastly noises. He kept it up until he reached the climax, when he would turn a complete somersault and lie flat amid the wreckage of the chairs, apparently quite satisfied for the moment. As time went on, however, these painful seizures grew gradually less frequent, and his friends tried to steer his mind into fresh channels. But his interest in other things didn’t seem to return, and he grew visibly listless and gloomy.

One fine morning it was Rat’s turn on guard, and he climbed the stairs to take over from Badger. He found Badger itching to get away and stretch his legs on a long tramp through his woods and along his own tunnels and burrows. “Toad’s still in bed,” Badger told him outside the door. “I can’t get anything out of him but, ‘Oh, leave me alone, I need nothing, maybe I’ll feel better soon, it may pass with time, please don’t worry,’ and so forth. Now mind yourself, Rat! When Toad is quiet and meek and acting like the hero of some Sunday-school storybook, that’s when he’s at his craftiest. He’s certainly up to something. I know him. Well, I really must go.”
“How are you today, old chap?” asked Rat cheerfully, as he came up to Toad’s bedside.

He had to wait several minutes before anything came back. Finally a weak voice answered, “Thank you ever so much, dear Ratty! How kind of you to ask! But first tell me how you are yourself, and how is the excellent Mole?”

“Oh, _we’ll_ be fine,” Rat answered. “Mole,” he added, without thinking, “is going for a jaunt with Badger. They won’t be back before lunch, so you and I can have a nice morning together, and I’ll do my best to entertain you. Come on now, up you get, there’s a good chap, and stop lying there sulking on such a lovely morning!”

“Dear, kind Rat,” Toad whispered, “you have no idea what state I’m in, or how far I am from ‘getting up’ at the moment—if I ever shall! But please don’t worry over me. I can’t bear being a burden to my friends, and I don’t expect to be one for much longer. In fact, I rather hope not.”

“Well, I hope not, too,” said Rat warmly. “You’ve caused us a dreadful amount of bother all this while, and I’m glad to hear that it’s going to end. And with weather like this, and the boating season only just starting! It’s really too bad of you, Toad! We don’t mind the trouble itself, but you’re making us miss so much.”

“I’m afraid it _is_ the bother that you mind, after all,” Toad replied in a feeble drawl. “I understand perfectly. It’s only natural. You’re worn out with fussing over me. I shouldn’t ask anything more of you. I know I’m a burden.”
“You certainly are,” said Rat. “But believe me, I’d put myself out for you in any way at all, if only you’d start behaving like a sensible animal.”

“If I could believe that, Ratty,” Toad whispered, weaker than ever, “then I would ask you—for the last time, very likely—to hurry round to the village as fast as you can—even now it may be too late—and bring the doctor. But never mind. It’s only a bother, and perhaps we should simply let things run their course.”
“Why on earth do you want a doctor?” asked Rat, stepping closer to look him over. Toad certainly lay very flat and still, and his voice was weaker, and he seemed a completely different animal.

“Surely you must have seen, lately——” Toad whispered. “But no—why should you? Noticing things is only a bother. Tomorrow, of course, you may find yourself thinking, ‘Oh, if only I had noticed sooner! If only I had done something!’ But no, it’s a bother. Never mind—forget I said anything.”

“Now look here, old man,” said Rat, starting to feel quite alarmed, “naturally I’ll bring you a doctor, if you truly believe you need one. But surely you can’t be as ill as all that yet. Let’s talk about something else.”

“I’m afraid, dear friend,” said Toad with a sorrowful smile, “that ‘talking’ will do very little in a case like this—and neither will doctors, for that matter. Still, a drowning animal clutches at any straw. And by the way—since you’re going anyway—I _hate_ to put you to more trouble, but I just remembered that you’ll walk right past the lawyer’s door—would you mind asking him to come up as well? It would be a comfort to me. There are times—perhaps I should say there is _a_ time—when a person must face unpleasant duties, no matter what it costs his worn-out constitution!”
“A lawyer! Oh, he must be truly ill!” the terrified Rat said to himself as he hurried out of the room, though he remembered to lock the door carefully behind him.
Out in the passage he stopped to think. The other two were miles away, and there was nobody he could ask.

“Better safe than sorry,” he decided after a moment. “I’ve seen Toad imagine himself dreadfully ill before, for no reason at all, but never once have I heard him ask for a lawyer! If nothing is really wrong, the doctor will tell him he’s a silly old fool and cheer him up, and that’s something gained. I’d best humor him and go. It won’t take long.” And off he ran to the village on his errand of mercy.

Toad had hopped lightly out of bed the moment he heard the key turn in the lock, and he watched Rat eagerly from the window until Rat disappeared down the carriage drive. Then, laughing heartily, he dressed as fast as he could in the smartest suit that came to hand, stuffed his pockets with money from a small drawer in the dressing table, and knotted the sheets from his bed into a makeshift rope. He tied one end around the middle post of the handsome Tudor window that was such a fine feature of his bedroom, scrambled out, slid easily to the ground, and set off in the opposite direction from Rat, marching along light-heartedly and whistling a cheerful tune.

It was a gloomy lunch for Rat when Badger and Mole finally came back, and he had to face them across the table with his pitiful, unconvincing story. You can imagine Badger’s sharp, even brutal, remarks, so we will skip them. But it hurt Rat that even Mole, though he took his friend’s side as far as he could, couldn’t help saying, “You’ve been a bit of a fool this time, Ratty! And Toad, of all animals!”
“He played his part awfully well,” said Rat, looking crushed.

“He played _you_ awfully well!” Badger shot back angrily. “Still, talking won’t fix anything. He’s gotten clean away for now, that much is certain. And the worst of it is, he’ll be so full of himself over what he thinks was his cleverness that he may do any sort of foolish thing. One comfort is that we’re free now, and don’t have to waste any more of our precious time standing guard. But we’d better keep sleeping at Toad Hall for a while longer. Toad may be brought back at any moment, on a stretcher or between two policemen.”

So Badger spoke, with no idea of what the future had in store, nor how much water, and how muddy and murky, would flow under the bridges before Toad would sit comfortably again in the Hall of his ancestors.

Meanwhile Toad, cheerful and carefree, was striding briskly along the high road, some miles from home. At first he had taken back paths, crossed many fields, and changed direction several times in case anyone was chasing him. But by now he felt safe from capture, the sun was smiling brightly down on him, and all of Nature seemed to join in a chorus of approval for the song of self-praise his own heart was singing, so he almost danced along the road in his satisfaction and conceit.

“That was a smart piece of work!” he said to himself, chuckling. “Brains against brute force, and brains came out on top, as they always do. Poor old Ratty! My, won’t he catch it when Badger gets back! A decent fellow, Ratty, with many good qualities, but very little intelligence and absolutely no education. I must take him in hand some day and see if I can make something of him.”

Stuffed full of conceited thoughts like these, he strode along with his head in the air until he reached a little town. There the sign of “The Red Lion,” swinging out over the road halfway down the main street, reminded him that he hadn’t had breakfast that day and was extremely hungry after his long walk. He marched into the inn, ordered the best lunch that could be got on such short notice, and sat down to eat it in the coffee room.

He was about halfway through his meal when a sound he knew only too well, coming down the street, made him jump and start trembling all over. The poop-poop! came closer and closer, the car could be heard turning into the inn yard and stopping, and Toad had to grab the leg of the table to hide his overwhelming emotion. Soon the party came into the coffee room, hungry, chatty and cheerful, going on and on about their morning’s adventures and the fine qualities of the machine that had carried them along so well. Toad listened eagerly, all ears, for a while, but at last he couldn’t bear it any longer. He slipped quietly out of the room, paid his bill at the bar, and as soon as he was outside strolled casually around to the inn yard. “There can’t be any harm,” he told himself, “in just _looking_ at it!”

The car stood in the middle of the yard with nobody watching it, since the stable hands and the other loungers were all at their dinner. Toad walked slowly around it, inspecting it, criticizing it, lost in deep thought.
“I wonder,” he said to himself after a while, “I wonder whether this kind of car _starts_ easily?”

The next moment, hardly knowing how it happened, he found he had hold of the crank handle and was turning it. As the familiar sound burst out, the old passion seized Toad and mastered him completely, body and soul. As if in a dream he found himself somehow sitting in the driver’s seat. As if in a dream he pulled the lever and swung the car around the yard and out through the archway. And, as if in a dream, every sense of right and wrong, every fear of the obvious consequences, seemed to be suspended for the time being. He picked up speed. As the car gobbled up the street and leapt out onto the high road through the open countryside, he was aware of only one thing. He was Toad once more, Toad at his best and highest, Toad the terror, the scatterer of traffic, the Lord of the lonely road. Everyone must give way before him or be struck into nothingness and everlasting night. He sang as he flew, and the car answered with a deep, humming drone. The miles were swallowed up beneath him as he raced he didn’t know where, following his instincts, living his hour, reckless of whatever might happen to him.

“It seems to me,” remarked the Chairman of the Bench of Magistrates cheerfully, “that the _only_ difficulty in this otherwise very clear case is how on earth we can make things hot enough for the incorrigible rogue and hardened ruffian we see cowering in the dock before us. Let me see: he has been found guilty, on the clearest evidence, first, of stealing a valuable motorcar; second, of driving in a way that endangered the public; and third, of gross impertinence to the country police. Mr. Clerk, would you please tell us the very stiffest penalty we can impose for each of these offenses? Without, of course, giving the prisoner the benefit of any doubt, because there isn’t any.”

The Clerk scratched his nose with his pen. “Some people would argue,” he remarked, “that stealing the motor-car was the gravest crime, and so it is. But insulting the police surely deserves the heaviest sentence, and so it should. Suppose you said twelve months for the theft, which is gentle. Suppose three years for the reckless driving, which is merciful. And suppose fifteen years for the insolence, and from what we heard in the witness-box it was a rather nasty piece of insolence, even if you believe only a tenth of what was said, and I never believe more than that myself. Then if I’ve added correctly, the total comes to nineteen years——”
“Excellent!” said the Chairman.
“—So you might as well round it up to a neat twenty years and be on the safe side,” the Clerk finished.

“A capital suggestion!” said the Chairman, nodding his approval. “Prisoner! Collect yourself and stand up straight. This time it will be twenty years. And take warning: if you ever come before us again, on any charge at all, we shall treat you very severely indeed!”

Then the brutal henchmen of the law fell upon the luckless Toad, loaded him with chains, and dragged him from the courthouse, shrieking, begging and protesting. They hauled him across the marketplace, where the playful crowd, always as hard on a caught criminal as they are sympathetic and helpful when someone is merely “wanted,” pelted him with jeers, carrots and popular catchphrases. They dragged him past hooting schoolchildren, their innocent faces lit up with the delight they always take in the sight of a gentleman in trouble. They went across the hollow-sounding drawbridge, beneath the spiked portcullis, and under the frowning archway of the grim old castle, whose ancient towers soared high overhead. They went past guardrooms full of grinning off-duty soldiers, and past sentries who coughed in a horrid, sarcastic way. That is as much as a sentry on duty dares to do to show his contempt and loathing of crime. They went up worn, winding stairs, past men-at-arms in steel helmets and breastplates, darting threatening looks through their visors. They crossed courtyards where mastiffs strained at their leashes and pawed the air to get at him. They passed aged guards, their halberds propped against the wall, dozing over a meat pie and a flagon of brown ale. On and on they went, past the rack chamber and the thumbscrew room, past the turning that led to the private scaffold, until they reached the door of the grimmest dungeon, deep in the heart of the innermost keep. There at last they stopped, where an ancient jailer sat fingering a bunch of enormous keys.

“Zounds!” said the police sergeant, taking off his helmet and wiping his forehead. “Wake up, thou old fool, and take from us this vile Toad, a criminal of deepest guilt and matchless cunning and resourcefulness. Watch and guard him with all thy skill; and mark thee well, graybeard, should anything go amiss, thy old head shall answer for his—and a plague on the pair of them!”

The jailer gave a grim nod and rested his shriveled hand on the shoulder of the wretched Toad. The rusty key groaned in the lock and the huge door slammed shut behind them. And Toad was a helpless prisoner, shut away in the deepest dungeon of the most closely guarded tower of the sturdiest castle in the whole length and breadth of Merry England.
